rules.message: A `setX(...)` state setter call appears LEXICALLY AFTER an async boundary (an `await`, or a `.then(`/`.catch(`/`.finally(` continuation) in the same function body, with no unmount/abort guard (`AbortController`/`AbortSignal`/`isMounted`/`mountedRef`/`signal:`/`cancelled`/`didCancel`) anywhere in that body — the reported line is the first setter that actually follows the boundary, not merely one that shares the function with it. THE GUARD VOCABULARY HAS TWO ARMS, and the second exists because the first is a hand-typed list of exact spellings and case-SENSITIVE: `cancelled` never matched `isCancelled`, the dominant React spelling, and a ref named `isDestroyed` was in no list at all (measured on getredash/redash @ ca79fe98: the second arm removed 12 of this rule's 35 findings there, every one a live guard with a cleanup, while that tree's one INERT guard kept reporting). The second arm is a SHAPE rather than a name: a flag whose identifier carries a cancel/abort/destroy/unmount/dispose stem, in any case, AND which is assigned `true` somewhere in the same body. A `stale` stem was in that list for one review cycle and was REMOVED, because a stem is a substring test and `stale` is cache-revalidation vocabulary rather than lifecycle vocabulary: an unrelated `let staleWhileRevalidate = true` inside the same effect silenced a genuinely unguarded setter (reproduced). The five that remain name teardown and nothing else. Demanding the assignment is what keeps the widening honest — a `let isCancelled = false` that nothing ever sets is an INERT guard (an effect returning no cleanup), the `if (!isCancelled)` wrapping the setter can never be false, and that finding is CORRECT and still fires, where a plain case-insensitive widening of the first arm would have silenced it. Two things the second arm still cannot do, stated rather than discovered: it does not prove WHERE the assignment happens, so a flag flipped on some non-cleanup path vetoes exactly as a cleanup does; and its stem list is still hand-written, so a project whose flag is named outside it (`bail`, `gone`) is not covered — those findings stay live rather than silently green, which is the direction a list of this kind should fail in. "Same function" means the NEAREST enclosing function, not the whole declaration: a boundary in a sibling closure no longer qualifies (measured on a 22-tree corpus: 6 of 87 findings changed — 4 dropped as sibling-closure or nested-callback pairings, 2 re-anchored onto a setter that genuinely follows a boundary in its own function), while a `.then(`/`.catch(`/`.finally(` continuation callback is scoped together with the call that schedules it, so a continuation setting state still fires. The flip side of that scoping: a setter inside a NESTED callback (a `.map`/`forEach`/`setTimeout`/event-handler closure) whose only boundary sits outside that callback no longer fires — an accepted under-report. The narrowing needs parser-projected function spans; a file whose spans could not be projected (parse failure, size cap, an external-parser envelope that omits them) keeps the old whole-declaration scope and its sibling-closure false positives. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. This is a TEXTUAL ORDER claim, not a dataflow one: it does not prove the setter runs on the resumed continuation (a setter in an `else` branch still counts, and so does one that follows a CONDITIONAL boundary — `if (stale) { await refresh(); }` then `setX(...)` fires even on the path where nothing was awaited), and it does NOT prove the component can unmount while the request is in flight (a plain event handler is mounted by construction whenever it fires, so a `setX(...)` inside one is an accepted false positive here). THAT PARENTHESIS DESCRIBES A GATE THIS RULE DOES NOT IMPLEMENT, AND THE `info` SEVERITY IS THAT ABSENCE MADE MACHINE-READABLE RATHER THAN LEFT IN PROSE. The discriminator that would earn a `warning` is whether the setter sits inside a `useEffect` callback (or a function one calls) — the only shape where teardown can land between the request and its resolve — and that gate is NOT EXPRESSIBLE by this matcher: the projected facts carry function bodies as ANONYMOUS line spans with no record of which call receives a function as its argument, and the TypeScript producer deliberately leaves a `useEffect` callback UNMERGED from its call site (its one merge is for `.then`/`.catch`/`.finally`, and widening it would re-create the sibling-closure pairing that merge exists to break). Measured over a 9-tree corpus: 34 of 49 findings sit in an event handler rather than an effect — 31 of one monorepo's 45, and BOTH findings in the two React-17 trees, so a React-VERSION gate would have preserved nothing but false positives. Read this band as advisory: a list to review, not a signal to break a build on. It stays `info` until the effect-containment gate is BUILT rather than described. SAME-LINE NESTING RESIDUAL (a MEASURED false negative, disclosed rather than fixed): on a single line "after" is decided by MATCH START OFFSET, so an `await` nested INSIDE the setter call's own argument list reads as coming AFTER it and does not pair — `setData(await fetch(url));` is silently NOT reported, while the two-statement spelling (`const r = await fetch(url); setData(r);`) fires, same file, same run. This is the mirror image of the `p.then(r => setX(r))` one-liner that DOES fire (there the boundary token starts first); closing it would need structural nesting awareness that a start-offset comparison between two independent regexes cannot have. But when the setter genuinely follows an in-flight await inside code that CAN unmount mid-request (an effect's async loader, a callback stored across a lifecycle boundary), the resolve races teardown: a stale-data flash overwriting newer state, or a wasted render right after remount. THE HEADLINE SYMPTOM IS VERSION-BOUND AND THIS RULE DOES NOT READ YOUR REACT VERSION: the console warning "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component" was REMOVED in React 18.0.0, because the update was always a silent no-op and the wording read as a leak report it never was. There is no memory leak on any version — below 18 the residual cost is that console line, at 18 and above it is wasted render work only. Thread an `AbortController` (or an `isMounted`/`mountedRef` flag) through the async function and skip the `setX(...)` call if the request was aborted or the component has unmounted. The `require_file` gate scopes this to React files (a `useEffect`/`useState` call, or a `from 'react'` import) to keep it out of non-component async helpers. The `setX(` trigger is anchored to a bare (non-member) call so a `localStorage.setItem`/`res.setHeader`/`date.setHours` is not mistaken for a state setter, and `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`setImmediate` are vetoed — so a genuine `setX(...)` that merely coexists with a timer in the same function is an accepted under-report.
